Computerised primary care records can be accessed to improve quality and to enable patient access to their records; but that consent for consent may be needed to access records for research.

computerised primary care data can improve patient access to records and monitoring of quality, but the issue of how to search records without knowing individual patient’s identity remains unresolved.

• Computerised primary care records are essential for patient record access, quality improvement and for research • The use of routinely collected primary data for research is controversial • The potential need to get consent from individual patients to look at their records to assess suitability is called ‘consent to consent’ • Consent is required for research but there is a debate about the need for consent to access records for the purposes of assessing eligibility for a study Computerised routinely collected data from primary care: essential for patient record,
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of methods that allow researchers to access routinely collected clinical data without compromising patient confidentiality.
the development of systems to allow patients convenient access to records, to monitor the quality of care, and to allow research to be conducted without compromising patient confidentiality.
the development, implementation and use of electronic patient records in primary care.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
routinely collected clinical data are an essential part of the fabric of our discipline and should be made available for research with appropriate consent and safeguards.
computerised routinely collected data are essential for the delivery of patient care and for quality improvement and research; and the need to obtain consent for consent is not required.
computerisation is essential for patient access, quality improvement and for research.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the computerisation of primary care data has been essential for the delivery of patient access to their records, quality improvement, and research.

we have shown that it is possible to search routinely collected data to identify people eligible for a particular clinical trial without anyone outside their GP practice knowing the patient's identity.
we need to find a balance between patient access, quality improvement, research and confidentiality.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to do research on anonymised records and that this is acceptable to patients.
the data can be used in a safe way, with the consent of a patient representative and without the need to contact the patient.
we can identify patients who might be eligible for a particular clinical study without anyone outside the practice knowing their identity.
